# Shared conventions

Every rimsky protocol shares these conventions. Read this page once, then read the guide for your protocol.

## The wire definitions

Rimsky ships ten `.proto` files declaring nine gRPC services, all in the protobuf package `rimsky.v1`.

| Proto file | Service it declares |
| --- | --- |
| `claim_producer.proto` | `ClaimProducer` |
| `claim_producer_observability.proto` | `ClaimProducerObservability` |
| `data_processing.proto` | `DataProcessing` |
| `events.proto` | none — event-log payload messages |
| `executor.proto` | `Executor` |
| `executor_observability.proto` | `ExecutorObservability` |
| `host_daemon.proto` | `HostDaemon` |
| `lifecycle.proto` | `LifecycleSubscriber` |
| `publisher.proto` | `Publisher` |
| `validation.proto` | `Validation` |

A gRPC method's full name is `/rimsky.v1.<Service>/<Method>`. Use that form when you probe a service by hand.

## Packages you can install

Rimsky publishes the wire contract as two packages plus the CLI.

**Go.** `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core/lib/protocols` is a module of its own, licensed Apache-2.0, and it imports nothing else from rimsky. Import it for the generated gRPC bindings, the claim-producer types, the enrollment client, the mutual-TLS helper, the HTTP+JSON bridge mounts, and the conformance libraries. The root module `github.com/rimsky-ai/rimsky-core` carries the orchestrator and the bundled services, and it is licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later or under a Fall Guy Consulting commercial license. Implement the protocols from your own process and you depend only on the Apache-2.0 module.

The packages a service author imports from the protocols module:

| Package | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `proto/v1/gen` | Generated clients, servers, and messages for all nine services |
| `claimproducer` | The `ClaimProducer` Go interface, `ClaimSpec`, `Capabilities`, write-semantics values |
| `lifecycle` | Request types for the lifecycle-subscriber callbacks |
| `serverkit` | `Listen`, `RunGRPC`, `GracefulStop`, and the HTTP+JSON bridge mounts |
| `serviceauth` | Enrollment, certificate renewal, and TLS-configured gRPC and HTTP servers |
| `enroll` | The raw `POST /v1/enroll` client and CA-pool helpers |
| `publisherkit` | Retrying message push into the control API |
| `config` | Strict YAML loading with environment expansion |
| `conformance/...` | The check suites the `rimsky conformance` subcommands run |
| `mtlstest` | Test helpers for mutual-TLS handshakes |

**npm.** `@rimsky-ai/protocols` ships the ten `.proto` files and nothing else executable. Its entry point exports exactly two things: `protoDir`, the directory holding the protos, and `protoPath(file)`, which joins a filename onto that directory. Point `@grpc/proto-loader` or another protobuf toolchain at them. The package ships no generated TypeScript stubs, so a TypeScript service author still runs a protobuf toolchain over the definitions.

**CLI.** Each GitHub release publishes `rimsky_<version>_linux_amd64.tar.gz`, `rimsky_<version>_linux_arm64.tar.gz`, `rimsky_<version>_darwin_amd64.tar.gz`, `rimsky_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz`, and `checksums.txt`. Each archive carries the `rimsky` binary, which is how you run the conformance suites.

## The capabilities handshake

Five of the nine services declare a `Capabilities` RPC: `ClaimProducer`, `ClaimProducerObservability`, `DataProcessing`, `ExecutorObservability`, and `Publisher`. Four do not: `Executor`, `Validation`, `LifecycleSubscriber`, and `HostDaemon`. A client that opens every connection with a `Capabilities` call gets `Unimplemented` from those four. Call `Capabilities` only where the protocol declares it.

An executor advertises itself through `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities`, not through `Executor`. That is why an executor with anything to declare — an attributes schema, tags, error classes — implements the observability sibling.

Rimsky performs the handshake at startup and when configuration reloads. It caches what you return and serves it back to operators on the observability read routes. Whatever you put in the handshake is what the deployment knows about you; there is no second registration step.

## Declaring your service to a deployment

An operator names your service in the deployment's configuration under the block matching its role: `executors`, `claim_producers`, `publishers`, `validators`, or `data_processors`. Each entry takes the same keys.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<block>.<name>.endpoint` | Where rimsky dials you |
| `<block>.<name>.observability_endpoint` | Where rimsky performs the capabilities handshake |
| `<block>.<name>.protocols` | The mix-in protocols this service also serves |
| `<block>.<name>.tls` | `off` or `required` |
| `executors.<name>.transport` | `grpc` or `http` — executors only |
| `claim_producers.<name>.write_semantics_allowed` | The envelope the producer may realize |

`protocols` accepts six values: `claim_producer`, `executor`, `publisher`, `lifecycle_subscriber`, `validation`, `data_processing`. Any other value stops the deployment at startup with `unknown protocol`.

`endpoint` must use the `grpc://` scheme for every block except an executor entry declaring `transport: http`. A claim-producer endpoint pointed at an HTTP bridge stops the deployment with `endpoint scheme must be grpc:// (got http://)`.

`tls: required` makes rimsky dial you with verified TLS. When the deployment turns on mutual TLS, every service entry defaults to `required` without the operator writing the key. A service that cannot present credentials against a `required` entry is reported unreachable, and nodes dispatched at it fail with a dial failure. Where the service is a claim producer, the deployment refuses to start at all rather than run unauthenticated.

## The HTTP+JSON bridge

Rimsky is a gRPC platform. One protocol is reachable over HTTP+JSON end to end, and two more have shipped bridge mounts that rimsky itself does not dial.

**Executor.** This is the full HTTP+JSON path. An operator writes `executors.<name>.transport: http` with an `http://` or `https://` endpoint, and rimsky dispatches by posting a protobuf-JSON `ExecuteRequest` to `POST <endpoint>/v1/Execute` with `Content-Type: application/json`. Your response body is a protobuf-JSON `Outcome`. Any non-2xx status fails the dispatch. Under `tls: required` the endpoint must use `https://` or the deployment refuses to start.

**Claim producer.** `serverkit.Mount` mounts seven routes on a `http.ServeMux`, one per verb: `POST /v1/capabilities`, `/v1/open`, `/v1/commit`, `/v1/abandon`, `/v1/release`, `/v1/split_scope`, `/v1/scopes_conflict`. Each takes the verb's protobuf-JSON request and returns its protobuf-JSON response. Rimsky never dials this bridge — a claim-producer endpoint must be `grpc://`. The bridge exists so you can drive your producer over HTTP, and `rimsky conformance claim-producer --transport http` runs the whole suite against it.

**Lifecycle subscriber.** `serverkit.MountLifecycle` mounts seven routes the same way: `POST /v1/on_template_registered`, `/v1/on_template_deployed`, `/v1/on_template_undeployed`, `/v1/on_template_deregistered`, `/v1/on_instance_created`, `/v1/on_instance_terminated`, `/v1/on_run_scope_terminal`. Rimsky dials lifecycle subscribers over gRPC only.

**Claim-producer observability.** `serverkit.MountObservability` mounts `GET /observability/v1/capabilities`, `GET /observability/v1/claims`, `GET /observability/v1/claims/...`, and `GET /observability/v1/admin/...`. Rimsky dials the gRPC service, not this bridge.

Both observability capabilities messages carry an `http_bridge_url` field. Rimsky records what you put there and republishes it on its observability read routes. It never dials the URL.

There is no HTTP+JSON path for `Validation`, `DataProcessing`, `Publisher`, or `HostDaemon`. Implement those over gRPC.

## Mutual-TLS enrollment

A deployment runs mutual TLS when its configuration sets `service_auth: mtls`. The default is `none`, and a deployment left on the default costs a service author nothing: no certificates, no trust store, no configuration.

Under `service_auth: mtls` your service obtains its own certificate at startup by exchanging an api-key for one. The exchange is the whole credential story — the operator manages one key per service and writes no certificate by hand.

### The two routes

`GET /v1/ca-root` returns the deployment CA's root certificate as PEM. It answers unauthenticated, because a service needs the root to verify the control API before it can present a token.

`POST /v1/enroll` exchanges your api-key for a leaf. Send `Authorization: Bearer <api-key>` and an optional JSON body `{"label": "<your-service-name>"}`. The response is JSON with `cert_pem`, `key_pem`, `ca_root_pem`, and `not_after`. The certificate's subject is the id of the key you enrolled with, and it lives 24 hours.

Both routes are mounted only when the deployment has a CA. On a deployment left at the default, both answer `404 page not found` — the router has no such path, rather than a handler refusing you. Under `service_auth: mtls`, `POST /v1/enroll` unauthenticated answers `403` with `enrollment requires an authenticated api-key principal`.

The key needs exactly one grant: `service:enroll`. Revoking that key ends the service's access — the enroll route refuses it, and a service restarted on it exits rather than serving without credentials.

### The environment variables your service reads

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `RIMSKY_SERVICE_AUTH` | `none` (default) or `mtls`. Any other value is a startup error. |
| `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL` | Base URL of the control API. Required under `mtls`. |
| `RIMSKY_API_KEY` | The api-key plaintext you enroll with. Required under `mtls`. |
| `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA` | Path to the PEM verifying the control API's certificate. Required when the control-API URL is `https://`. |
| `RIMSKY_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_ENROLLMENT` | Set to accept an `http://` control-API URL under `mtls`. |

Enrollment fails closed in three ways. Under `mtls` with an `http://` control-API URL and no override, your service refuses to start, because the api-key would cross that hop in the clear against an unverified server. Under `mtls` with an `https://` URL and no `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA`, it refuses for the same reason. Setting `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA` alongside a non-`https` URL is also a startup error, since a pinned root cannot secure a plaintext hop. Set `RIMSKY_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_ENROLLMENT=1` only on a trusted local network; the values `0`, `false`, and `no` mean off.

The deployment operator supplies the CA's own encryption key in `RIMSKY_CA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, as 32 bytes of standard base64. That variable belongs to the control API, not to your service.

### Renewal

Your service re-enrolls before its certificate expires. The renewal deadline sits at two-thirds of the certificate's lifetime, and the check runs every minute. A restart re-enrolls from the same key and gets a fresh certificate. The operator touches nothing.

### Using it from Go

```go
identity, err := serviceauth.LoadFromEnv(ctx, "my-service")
if err != nil {
    return err                       // fail closed: no credentials, no service
}
identity.StartMaintain(ctx, "my-service")

srv := identity.GRPCServer()         // mutual TLS when enabled, plaintext when not
genv1.RegisterExecutorServer(srv, myExecutor)

lis, err := serverkit.Listen(host, port)
serverkit.RunGRPC(ctx, srv, lis, "my-service")
```

`identity.GRPCServer()` requires and verifies a client certificate from the deployment CA on every inbound call, and returns a plain gRPC server when service authentication is off. `identity.OutboundHTTPClient(timeout)` presents your leaf on outbound calls and pins the deployment root; it returns `nil` when service authentication is off, so fall back to your own client. `identity.ServerOnlyTLSConfig()` serves your certificate without demanding one back, for a listener facing clients outside the deployment.

## Ports

A service reads its own port from its own environment variable. One variable overrides them all: when `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` is set, bind there. The host daemon sets it when it spawns your binary as a late-bound service, and there is no handshake back — a binary that binds elsewhere fails the readiness poll. A malformed `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` is a startup error rather than a silent fallback.

## Error classes

An error class is a string your service chooses. A template author routes on it by name.

Advertise your classes in your capabilities handshake — `declared_error_classes` on `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities` and on `ClaimProducer.Capabilities`. Rimsky checks a template's `error_types` keys against what you declared and warns on a key outside your vocabulary. The class you raise at run time then selects the template's policy for it.

Two conventions matter when you pick names.

Prefix your classes with your service's name, as `http/network_error` or `agent/attribute_invalid`. Rimsky's own classes carry no prefix: `template_resolution_failed`, `template_validation_failed`, `executor_schema_unavailable`, `attributes_schema_failed`, `unresolved_executor`, `executor_sync_timeout`, `executor_protocol_violation`, and `abandoned`. Those eight are first-class vocabulary a template author may route on.

Prefix wildcards do not work. A template author writing `error_types: {"http/*": ...}` gets a policy that registers with a warning and never fires — routing matches the exact class string. The one accepted wildcard is `acquire/*`, the synthetic family rimsky raises for acquisition failures, and it is not an emitter prefix. Declare and raise exact class names, and tell your users to route on exact names.

## Health

Rimsky does not require a health endpoint, and there is no shared path. Two listeners in the whole shipped set answer `GET /health`. If you want a liveness probe, mount one and tell your operators its path.
